[2] Closing a connection (using `close()`), or unsubscribing from a subscription, are generally considered immediate requests. When you close or unsubscribe the library will halt messages in any pending queue or cache for subscribers. When you drain a subscription or connection, it will process any inflight and cached/pending messages before closing. Drain provides clients that use queue subscriptions with a way to bring down applications without losing any messages. A client can bring up a new queue member, drain and shut down the old queue member, all without losing messages sent to the old client.

[2] [3] You can get notified when a JetStream message has used up all its retries, specifically via advisory messages. When a message reaches its maximum number of delivery attempts, an advisory message is published on the `$JS.EVENT.ADVISORY.CONSUMER.MAX_DELIVERIES.<STREAM>.<CONSUMER>` subject, containing a `stream_seq` field that allows retrieval of the specific message by sequence number. To implement a dead letter queue, you can listen to these advisory messages to manage and process messages that have been considered un-re-deliverable.

[1] JetStream provides decoupled flow control over streams, the flow control is not 'end to end' where the publisher(s) are limited to publish no faster than the slowest of all the consumers (i.e. the lowest common denominator) can receive but is instead happening individually between each client application (publishers or consumers) and the nats server. When using the JetStream publish calls to publish to streams there is an acknowledgment mechanism between the publisher and the NATS server, and you have the choice of making synchronous or asynchronous (i.e. 'batched') JetStream publish calls. On the subscriber side, the sending of messages from the NATS server to the client applications receiving or consuming messages from streams is also flow controlled. NATS clients shuffle the server list on reconnect to prevent a _thundering herd_ situation where all clients try to reconnect to the same server immediately, causing a denial of service attack. To confirm that the server has received published messages, a client uses [PING/PONG interaction] [2]. When an application calls flush, most libraries will put a PING on the outgoing queue of messages, and wait for the server to respond with a PONG before saying that the flush was successful.

Regarding whether these pings count against the outstanding ping limit, [2] states that pings sent this way do not count towards [max outgoing pings] [2], indicating that they do not count against the outstanding ping limit.

[4] By default a NATS connection will echo messages if the connection also has interest in the published subject. This means that if a publisher on a connection sends a message to a subject any subscribers on that same connection will receive the message. Clients can opt to turn off this behavior, such that regardless of interest, the message will not be delivered to subscribers on the same connection. The NoEcho option can be useful in BUS patterns where all applications subscribe and publish to the same subject.

[3] The default value for the `connection_rate_limit` is 0, which disables the limit. Setting it to a higher value would then determine the number of new TLS client connections a single server can accept before rejecting new connections, capped at that number in any one second window. Therefore, out of the box with the default of 0, a single NATS server will accept no new client connections based on the `connection_rate_limit` setting.
